title: Some 'classic' money advice is actually pretty new—and not all of it is worthwhile, says historian

body: In the world of personal finance, many of the lessons we're taught are touted as historical. Since the dawn of time, the experts tell us, those who got ahead financially lived within their means, saved diligently and spent and invested carefully.It made Joseph Moore — a historian and author of "How to Get Rich in American History," published in April — wonder if Americans had been receiving, following and prospering from the same advice for the past few centuries. What he found surprised him."Is there timeless wisdom of money that we should all be following, from Ben Franklin to now? The answer is no," Moore says. "It turns out, what 'always' worked is always changing."Some common financial principles that seem old are recent phenomena, Moore says, and some situations that seem new are, in fact, quite common throughout history.In both such cases, knowing your history can be helpful. After all, if previous generations flourished without more recent advice, maybe the current wisdom isn't as valuable as we think. Conversely, maybe you don't need to find a creative solution to a problem that isn't actually that novel.Here are three misconceptions Moore points out from the history of American personal finance — and what you can learn from them.Housing shortages aren't newAmericans are struggling with housing affordability amid high mortgage rates and rising home prices. But it's not a historically unique problem, Moore says."We absolutely are in a housing crisis caused by a housing shortage," he says. "It's neither the first nor the worst."Moore points to 1948, when the ratio of people who wanted to buy a house to available inventory was about double what it is now, as the worst culprit. The year 1981, when the median new mortgage consumed more than half of the median household income, was no picnic either, he says.That doesn't mean that the current shortage isn't real or that you should suck it up because other people had it worse, Moore says. But it is worth looking at how people have historically solved it — personally, not politically. And in the case of a housing shortage, Moore's answers aren't glamorous. One historical solution was moving more often. Currently, the housing market is worse in some places than others. Folks used to be more likely to pick up and go to places where opportunities were better, Moore says. For most of the country's history, between 1 in 3 and 1 in 5 Americans moved every year, he says, pointing to research by historian and journalist Yoni Appelbaum. Now, it's more like 1 in 13, Moore notes.Another common solution for unaffordable homes: sharing housing. In 19th-century America, it wasn't at all uncommon for homeowners to rent out rooms in their house to help with the mortgage, Moore says. The same logic applies to modern-day renters who split spaces with roommates to keep costs down, he says."It's a shortage of space, so you have to monetize space," says Moore.Diversification and compounding weren't the historical path to wealthInvestors are often told that the path to long-term wealth is simple: Invest consistently in a low-cost, broadly diversified stock portfolio. Need proof? Consider the S&P 500's upward trajectory since before the stock market crash in 1929, and think of all the compounding returns you could have earned over that period had you invested."Something really new that we act like is really old is that compound interest is what builds wealth," Moore says. "Nobody got rich by compound interest for most of U.S. history, and if they did, they were generally already wealthy."Think about it: Index funds weren't around, nor were fractional shares. If you wanted to own every stock in an index, you'd need to have the money to buy shares of each, plus a fee for your broker, of course. "For most of American history, less than 10% of Americans owned stocks at all. That's not how people got wealthy," Moore says. "They got wealthy by concentrating most of their efforts in small businesses and careers, real estate and job tools. [Few people] compounded their way to wealth until the greatest generation and baby boomers, when the technology came online to allow you to use compounding."Investors should still take advantage of the innovations that made diversified, low-cost portfolios widely accessible, Moore says. Just remember that there's more than one way to build wealth.People used to keep budgeting simpleOne piece of financial advice that feels tried and true is to create a budget and stick to it. How else can you make sure you don't overspend and keep yourself on track toward your financial goals?But Moore says that the household spending spreadsheet is a relatively new phenomenon."Nobody in the 1800s budgeted the way we talk about budgeting," he says. "These forward-facing spending categories would be completely foreign to anyone's thinking."For most of American history, what folks did instead was look at their money in big buckets. A couple might divide things between the husband's and wife's income, for instance, he says. Or, to keep things even simpler, they divided income between what they needed to survive, and whatever was leftover. More complex budgeting schemes came into fashion in the early 20th century, Moore says, with financial guides at the time touting how much you could save by slashing the likes of alcohol and tobacco — the lattes and avocado toast of their day.There's no one right way to manage money. But if you find budgeting tedious, Moore argues that attitude puts you in line with generations of Americans who kept things simple by practicing what we'd now call reverse budgeting: paying their bills, putting money away for goals and then spending the rest as they saw fit.

schema.headline: Some 'classic' money advice is actually pretty new—and not all of it is worthwhile, says historian

title: Trump says 'if Ken Paxton loses' Texas Senate race, blame Cornyn and Karl Rove
description: US President Donald Trump speaks in the Rose Garden at the White House, Washington DC, Oct. 15, 2026. Jim Watson | AFP | Getty ImagesPresident Donald
body: US President Donald Trump speaks in the Rose Garden at the White House, Washington DC, Oct. 15, 2026. Jim Watson | AFP | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Thursday said that if Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton loses, it will be the fault of incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn and conservative commentator Karl Rove.Trump accused Cornyn and Rove of "doing everything possible to make it hard" for Paxton, the state's attorney general, to beat Democratic nominee James Talarico. Cornyn lost the Republican primary to Paxton, whom Trump controversially endorsed."If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career," Trump wrote on Truth Social.Trump's preemptive blame-casting came as Texas has surprisingly become one of the most competitive battlegrounds of the 2026 midterm cycle. Most recent polls show state Rep. Talarico maintaining a lead in the low-to-mid single digits over Paxton.The reliably red state has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1988. In 2024, Texans voted for Trump over Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris by nearly 14 percentage points.Cornyn's office and Rove did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on Trump's post.Trump's decision to back Paxton in the GOP primary delivered a major blow to the four-term incumbent Cornyn, whom the president viewed as disloyal. The move was also seen as a major gamble, as Paxton's history of scandal and opposition within his own party has made him a polarizing figure.Hoping to stave off Democrats' goal of winning majority control of the Senate, groups backing Republicans have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the Texas contest, making it the most expensive race of the cycle.GOP spending in the race has topped $370 million so far, eclipsing Democratic spending by nearly $235 million, according to AdImpact.Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Rove, calling him a "loser" and urging Fox News to stop putting him on air.Rove, who was a senior advisor to former President George W. Bush, "is so bad for the Republican Party, and completely wrong so often," Trump wrote in a Sept. 14 Truth Social post.In a Wall Street Journal op-ed two days later, Rove said that he would back a Democratic candidate in a different race in Texas, voting blue for just the second time in his life.

schema.headline: Trump says 'if Ken Paxton loses' Texas Senate race, blame Cornyn and Karl Rove

title: Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity
description: The Porsche Mission S concept car.Courtesy PorschePorsche on Thursday revealed a concept car called Mission S that signals a new design direction and
body: The Porsche Mission S concept car.Courtesy PorschePorsche on Thursday revealed a concept car called Mission S that signals a new design direction and flagship model for the famed German sports carmaker.The debut of the sleek midengine vehicle is part of a turnaround plan revealed last week by the Volkswagen-controlled brand that includes efforts to boost profits through higher-end products and lower vehicle sales.Porsche described Mission S as "a first glimpse of the brand's evolved design identity" that also represents a "super sports car platform" that will be positioned above its iconic 911 sports car.The vehicle's design is recognizably Porsche but with more aggressive styling compared with its current models, including new hood vents and a roof scoop. Its rear features more differentiated flair in which the vehicle's spoiler flows into its rear panels.The rear of the Porsche Mission S concept car.Courtesy Porsche"A Porsche must be recognisable as a Porsche at first glance," Porsche Chairman Michael Leiters said in a release. "The Mission S provides a glimpse of the ideas and design features that will shape Porsche in the coming years."Automakers routinely use concept vehicles to gauge customer interest, showcase future technologies and signal the direction of a vehicle or brand.The company did not release expected pricing or performance specifications for such future models. Starting prices for its current 911 models range from roughly $135,500 for an entry-level Carrera to more than $203,000 for a Carrera 4 GTS convertible.The interior of the Porsche Mission S concept car.Courtesy PorscheDuring Porsche's capital markets day on Oct. 7, the company outlined its "Sportwagenschmiede '35" turnaround plan, which focuses on emphasizing high-end sports cars and luxury SUVs to get the carmaker back on track. Porsche's operating margin last year was only 1.1%, compared with 14.1% in 2024, as the company deals with increased costs, U.S. tariffs and declining sales in China.The turnaround plan includes a long-term target for a group ‌operating margin of 15% and a midterm breakeven point of 200,000 units or below annually. That compares with sales of 279,449 in 2025.

schema.headline: Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity

title: India's rupee forecast to weaken toward 100-per-dollar level even as RBI pushes back
description: A man holds an Indian one hundred rupee (below) and a US dollar currency note at a foreign exchange office in Hyderabad on May 16, 2026. (Photo by Noa
body: A man holds an Indian one hundred rupee (below) and a US dollar currency note at a foreign exchange office in Hyderabad on May 16, 2026. (Photo by Noah SEELAM / AFP via Getty Images)Noah Seelam | Afp | Getty ImagesFund outflows and a rising energy bill are expected to keep putting pressure on India's rupee, even as the central bank works to slow depreciation.Over the last several days, the currency has recovered from 96.79 rupees per dollar to the 95-level, aided by the Reserve Bank of India's latest measures. But while those will provide short-term relief, the currency is expected to weaken toward the end of the year and mid-2027, and a 100 rupee-per-dollar mark could not be ruled out, strategists said.The RBI's steps will slow the rupee's depreciation, but they cannot "fully offset the fundamental pressures stemming from elevated oil prices, a wider current account deficit, and a challenging global capital flow environment," Hanna Luchnikava-Schorsch, head of Asia-Pacific economics at S&P Global Market Intelligence, told CNBC.Her firm sees the Indian currency trading around 97 per US dollar by end-2026 and at 98 rupees by mid-2027. Singapore-based Mizuho Securities also expects the rupee to slide to 98 rupees against the greenback by late 2026 and early next year, Vishnu Varathan, head of macro strategy for APAC at the firm, told CNBC."The RBI is determined to do whatever is necessary to ensure orderly movement in the foreign exchange market," Sanjay Malhotra, the governor of the RBI, said in an interview with local Indian media outlet Moneycontrol on Tuesday.Curbs on FX speculationOn Saturday, the central bank announced measures that will make it expensive to take speculative bets on the rupee and restrict rebooking of cancelled foreign exchange derivative contracts.  It also opened a special window to meet the entire daily dollar requirements of three public sector oil marketing companies, ring-fencing this trade from spot markets.The steps offer "short-term to medium-term stability, not long-term structural support," Devarsh Vakil, head of research at HDFC Securities, told CNBC,Stock Chart IconStock chart iconThese steps come just months after the central bank in June launched a special scheme, known as the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits, that offered incentives to non-resident Indians for making foreign currency deposits in Indian banks.While this boosted the RBI's foreign exchange reserves by $105 billion, global adverse conditions forced the central bank to make "aggressive" intervention in spot markets to counter the pressure on the rupee, global brokerage Nomura said in a report on Saturday.Since the close of the program on Aug. 30, the rupee has fallen 1.9% against the dollar, and the RBI's interventions to curb the decline "through dollar sales" have resulted in foreign reserves falling by $51 billion as of Oct. 2, Indian brokerage Ambit Capital said in a report on Wednesday.  FCNR-B, along with other currency swap measures announced in June, has led to forward dollar commitments of $200 billion that reduce the RBI's effective reserve cover, "leaving the rupee vulnerable to further depreciation," the report said.India's import cover stands at around 6.2 months, its lowest since the U.S. taper tantrum in 2013, it added.2027 OutlookIndia, which remains the world's fastest-growing major economy, is among the countries most vulnerable to supply disruptions caused by the Iran war. The South Asian country meets nearly 85% of its fuel needs via imports, with the Strait of Hormuz being a key supply route before the war.High energy costs, coupled with record exits of foreign investors from its capital markets due to risk aversion and the lack of artificial intelligence play, have kept the rupee under pressure. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi appealed to citizens last month to avoid foreign travel and buying gold, to ease the pressure on the local currency. He had made a similar call in May, amid the growing risks to the economy from the Iran war.A move towards 100 rupees per US dollar cannot be excluded, Luchnikava-Schorsch said, adding that the scenario could play out "if oil prices rise further, portfolio outflows resume and the current account deficit widens beyond current expectations."Foreign portfolio investors have sold direct Indian equities worth $32.5 billion this year through Oct. 13, according to the data of Indian depository NSDL.The rupee is likely to remain under pressure for the financial year ending in March 2027, Harsimran Sahni, associate director and head of treasury at Indian firm Anand Rathi Global Finance, said."Businesses should strengthen their hedging strategies and stress-test their foreign currency exposures," Sahni said, adding that RBI interventions can moderate volatility but cannot offset external imbalances "indefinitely."If sustained capital outflows coincide with elevated crude prices and a widening current account deficit, the rupee could move toward the 100 per dollar mark, he said.

schema.headline: India's rupee forecast to weaken toward 100-per-dollar level even as RBI pushes back

title: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt
description: Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesCoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names. CoreWeave
body: Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesCoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names. CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago. Coreweave's 5-year credit default swap spreadCredit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive. Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%. While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power. Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier. The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.  Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCoreWeave's five-day performanceNo one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive. "It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said. 'Self-fulfilling prophecy'CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC."When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity. "The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research. Oracle's 5-year credit default swaps spreadDomino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week."A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

schema.headline: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

title: Netflix Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria is leaving, will be replaced by Peter Rice
description: Bela Bajaria at Netflix's " A House of Dynamite" premiere held at The Egyptian Theatre Hollywood on Oct. 9, 2025 in Los Angeles, California.Jesse Gran
body: Bela Bajaria at Netflix's " A House of Dynamite" premiere held at The Egyptian Theatre Hollywood on Oct. 9, 2025 in Los Angeles, California.Jesse Grant | Variety | Getty ImagesNetflix on Thursday announced Bela Bajaria will be replaced as the company's chief content officer by former Disney exec Peter Rice, effective Oct. 26.Rice most recently oversaw Disney's cable channels, news programming and coverage of major sporting events."Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry," co-CEO Ted Sarandos said in a statement. "I'm excited to welcome him to Netflix as Chief Content Officer as we continue to scale and deliver members more of the stories they love."Before Rice was at Disney, he held roles at 21st Century Fox and Fox Searchlight Pictures. Netflix in its announcement called him "one of the entertainment industry's most respected creative executives." In his new role, Rice will oversee the company's global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events."[Netflix has] shown again and again that they're willing to take chances on distinctive voices and fresh ideas, and I'm excited to work with the team to help bring even more great stories to members everywhere," he said in a statement.watch nowBajaria, who is leaving Netflix after nearly 10 years, most recently led the company's global content team. She had been focused on the company's live sports strategy, looking to create events out of buzzy games and tournaments. "I'm incredibly grateful for everything she's done to help Netflix entertain the world," Sarandos said in a statement.The announcement comes a day after Netflix instituted layoffs across its organization, eliminating approximately 6% of its workforce, or roughly 1,000 jobs. Shares of the company are down more than 20% this year, though the stock remained relatively unchanged in extended trading Thursday. The media company will report its next quarterly earnings on Tuesday.

schema.headline: Netflix Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria is leaving, will be replaced by Peter Rice

title: Economists: Hot PPI shows Fed's work is not done
description: A customer with a loaded shopping cart of groceries at a Walmart Supercenter retail store in North Bergen, New Jersey, U.S., Nov. 21, 2025.  Mike Sega
body: A customer with a loaded shopping cart of groceries at a Walmart Supercenter retail store in North Bergen, New Jersey, U.S., Nov. 21, 2025.  Mike Segar | ReutersWall Street estimates for the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation indicator now expect an acceleration from the level that prompted the central bank to hike rates last month.The estimates come after a hotter-than-expected producer price index came in at 1.3% Thursday, the biggest monthly gain since March 2022 and more than double the 0.6% consensus.That drove the year-over-year increase to 6.3%, the biggest jump since December 2022. The increase was paced by a 20% rise in gasoline prices. But taking out food, energy and trade services, prices still rose a healthy 0.5%, indicating that inflation was broader than just energy. Seven Wall Street estimates gathered by CNBC show core personal consumption expenditures inflation for September, which will be published later this month, is forecast to rise 0.32%, up from 0.25% in August. Wall Street economists use the consumer price index, released Wednesday, and the PPI to estimate the PCE. "We see real risks the Fed will deliver another rate hike in two weeks' time even as recent Fedspeak tempered expectations for back-to-back increases,'' wrote Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide. Several Fed officials have argued that the Fed does not need to hurry to hike rates, though they have suggested more rate hikes are needed. As a result, Fed futures on Thursday showed just a 29% probability of a hike at the Fed meeting at the end of this month, but a 91% probability of at least one hike by December. A 0.32% increase in PCE would boost the year-over-year core inflation rate to 3.1%, up from 3.01% in August. Estimates ranged from a high of 0.35% from Barclays to a low of 0.29% from Oxford Economics. "The picture is not benign with inflation elevated and intensifying," wrote Alex Pelle, senior U.S. economist at Mizuho Securities. "On the economic data alone, there is little reason for the Fed to hesitate to continue moving the policy rate higher."Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has suggested one litmus test for not hiking is confidence that inflation will return in a timely manner to the Fed's 2% target. Both headline and core PCE inflation have been above target since 2021. They have inched steadily higher since tariffs were introduced in April 2025. The gains have accelerated since the beginning of the Iran war.The Fed prefers the PCE because, compared to the CPI, it believes it more closely resembles how Americans actually spend their money and changes its weightings when consumers change their spending patterns.

schema.headline: Economists: Hot PPI shows Fed's work is not done

title: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
description: A view of a KFC restaurant in Vallejo, California.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesKFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beve
body: A view of a KFC restaurant in Vallejo, California.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesKFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes. "This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."Beverage cups stacked inside a Yum Brands KFC restaurant in Shelbyville, Kentucky, Jan. 29, 2021.Luke Sharrett | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFor many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House, its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas. Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands. It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway, the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

schema.headline: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades

title: Harvard’s endowment jumps 27% in fiscal 2026, lifted by SpaceX as top holding
description: Students walk on campus at Harvard University, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Nov. 19, 2025.Reba Saldanha | ReutersHarvard University's endowment grew 2
body: Students walk on campus at Harvard University, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Nov. 19, 2025.Reba Saldanha | ReutersHarvard University's endowment grew 27.1% in fiscal year 2026, its strongest return in five years, the school said in its annual financial report released on Thursday. The endowment, which beat the S&P 500's 22.3% total return in the same period by 4.8 percentage points, now totals nearly $68 billion. The outperformance came amid actions by the Trump administration to penalize the school and withhold funding from the university. "While markets can easily take back what they give, that return will strengthen the endowment's capacity to support the University over time," Harvard's chief financial officer Ritu Kalra and treasurer Timothy Barakett wrote in the 49-page annual report. "The University deliberately smooths distributions so that operating support does not rise and fall with the markets. Strong investment returns therefore support Harvard's work gradually, through future distributions."The returns marked the best year for the endowment, managed by the Harvard Management Company, since 2021. Harvard's fiscal year ends on June 30. In its second-quarter 13F filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Harvard unveiled a $2.2 billion stake in Elon Musk's SpaceX rocket and satellite company. It marked the endowment's largest single holding by value, trailed by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company at just under $350 million. Harvard's financial picture, though, is undermined by moves by the federal government. Federally-sponsored research revenue declined 19.5% to $509 million in fiscal 2026. And starting in the current fiscal year, "endowment resources will face an additional constraint, with the federal excise tax on Harvard's net investment income rising nearly six-fold, from 1.4% to 8%," Kalra and Barakett wrote. "We estimate the higher rate will cost roughly $300 million a year.""[I]n a year of returns like this one," the federal excise tax "would be several times larger," they noted.President Alan Garber acknowledged such headwinds, but said in the report that Harvard can still succeed."Together, we have the opportunity to set the University on a path to excellence that none of us can imagine today," he said. "Notwithstanding the challenges and uncertainty, this is a thrilling time to be part of a great American institution devoted to Veritas."

schema.headline: Harvard’s endowment jumps 27% in fiscal 2026, lifted by SpaceX as top holding

title: Democrat Talarico says he raised record $64 million over summer in Texas Senate race
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a “Talarico for Texas: Frontera Tour” campaign rally at the International Center For Tra
body: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a “Talarico for Texas: Frontera Tour” campaign rally at the International Center For Trade convention center on July 13, 2026 in Eagle Pass, Texas. Brandon Bell | Getty ImagesDemocratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico raised $64 million in the third quarter, his campaign announced Thursday, setting what the campaign said is a Senate fundraising record as Republicans pour outside money into the race to bolster GOP nominee Ken Paxton in the 2026 midterm election.The haul was the largest ever reported by a Senate candidate in the July-through-September quarter, according to the campaign, surpassing the previous record of $57 million set by South Carolina Democrat Jaime Harrison, who unsuccessfully ran against Republican Lindsey Graham in 2020.Talarico has raised more than $134 million since launching his campaign last year, according to his campaign ahead of the quarterly filing deadline with the Federal Election Commission.“Grassroots contributors from across Texas are coming together to end billionaire control over our politics and bring down costs for working families,” Talarico said in a statement.The campaign said more than 1.3 million people have donated and that 97% of contributions were $100 or less. Paxton, by comparison, announced earlier this month that his campaign and two affiliated fundraising committees raised a combined $18 million during the quarter.The candidates' full financial picture will become clearer after their quarterly reports are filed with the FEC. The filings will show how much each campaign spent and how much cash they had left entering the final stretch.But the gap in direct fundraising tells only part of the financial story. Republican outside groups have spent more than $175 million since Sept. 1 supporting Paxton or attacking Talarico, according to AdImpact, helping offset Paxton's weaker campaign fundraising. Overall political advertising in the race has surpassed $500 million.SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk has emerged as a major force in the race, giving $10 million to a pro-Paxton super PAC, according to figures confirmed Monday by a spokesman for Musk's America PAC,  while his America PAC has spent about $9.4 million attacking Talarico and another $1.8 million supporting Paxton, according to FEC filings.   The source of that money matters as federal law guarantees candidates lower broadcast rates for television advertising than super PACs, allowing Talarico's campaign dollars to go further in buying TV exposure than outside Republican groups.No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994, and the party has not won a U.S. Senate race there since 1988. But Talarico leads Paxton 48.5% to 45.2% in FiftyPlusOne's polling average, a 3.3-percentage point advantage, forcing Republicans to devote significant resources to what has traditionally been safe territory.Talarico's fundraising also eclipses previous high-water marks for Texas Democrats. Beto O'Rourke raised $38.1 million in the third quarter of 2018 during his challenge to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.

schema.headline: Democrat Talarico says he raised record $64 million over summer in Texas Senate race

title: Russia returns to G20 table in Bangkok on U.S. invitation that angers Europe
description: ASHEVILLE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 1: Miniter of Finance for Russia Anton Siluanov sits in a plenary session on sovereign debt hosted by Treasury S
body: ASHEVILLE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 1: Miniter of Finance for Russia Anton Siluanov sits in a plenary session on sovereign debt hosted by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent for the 2026 G20 Financial meetings on September 1, 2026 in Asheville, North Carolina.  Melissa Sue Gerrits | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesRussia's finance minister attended a Group of 20 meeting in Bangkok on Thursday, his second in-person appearance at the event since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, testing how far Washington's rapprochement with Moscow will strain ties with Europe. Anton Siluanov and Bank of Russia Deputy Governor Elizaveta Danilova were listed as Russia's delegates at the finance ministers and central bank governors' meetings on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, according to a seating plan seen by CNBC. Siluanov was in the meeting, according to a person familiar with the matter. According to the layout document, Russian delegates were seated between attendees from South Korea and the United Arab Emirates. German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil was also listed as an attendee. At the August G20 finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, he told Siluanov that Moscow must end the war and declined to pose in a group photo with him. The traditional group photo was ultimately taken without the Russian delegation after European officials protested. Klingbeil has pushed back on the U.S. efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage, reportedly saying after the Thursday meeting that "there will be no pretending that Russia is now returning as a normal member of the G20 and simply taking its seat at the table again — not with me, and not with the other Europeans."Russia's seat at the table tests how far Washington can ease pressure on Moscow without breaking with its European allies. The U.S., which took over the G20 presidency this year, welcomed Russia's finance minister back to the finance talks after years of isolation over the invasion of Ukraine.  The Trump administration also introduced a deal to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel imports until April, drawing criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies. Dombrovskis told CNBC on Wednesday that "now it's not a time to ease sanctions on Russia." watch nowIn a statement issued after the Thursday meetings, Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers said Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on commercial vessels "must end." Those impacts "are exacerbated by Russia's unprovoked and unjustifiable war in Ukraine," he said, adding that Australia calls for Russia to end the war and respect Ukraine's sovereignty. The finance chiefs ended the meeting without a joint communique, underscoring persistent divisions among members over the Middle East conflict, trade imbalances, and Russia's war with Ukraine. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who would normally chair the talks, skipped the meetings to stay in Washington. The Asheville meeting also ended without a communique, after China objected to language on several issues, including efforts to rectify excessive global trade surpluses. The U.S. instead issued a chair's statement backed by every member present except China, with Bessent calling China "the dissenter."Delegates started the day with a plated breakfast of baked goat cheese, spinach and egg soufflé with chutney made from locally grown Bijin tomatoes, according to a menu card at the venue. The bread basket came with "Nam Dok Mai" mango jam. Every card carried the U.S. presidency's stars-and-stripes G20 logo and its "Freedom 250" tagline, marking America's 250th anniversary. The finance ministers' meeting Thursday could have helped lay the groundwork for improved coordination on a raft of global challenges, including energy problems stemming from the Middle East conflict and concerns about record public debt in advanced economies. Leaders are expected to convene at the next G20 summit in Miami in December.

schema.headline: Russia returns to G20 table in Bangkok on U.S. invitation that angers Europe

title: U.S. sues California in fight over checking citizenship of mail voters
description: A voter drops a mail-in ballot at an official drop box inside City Hall during a primary election in San Francisco, California, on Tuesday, June 2, 20
body: A voter drops a mail-in ballot at an official drop box inside City Hall during a primary election in San Francisco, California, on Tuesday, June 2, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe federal government sued the state of California on Thursday in an escalating battle over how to prevent non-U.S. citizens from voting by mail in federal elections.The  lawsuit is the latest action by the Department of Justice targeting state administration of elections, which President Donald Trump has often criticized as susceptible to fraud and voting by noncitizens.The civil complaint, which the DOJ had threatened to file, asks a judge to prevent California officials from tabulating mail-in ballots "from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined."The Department of Justice asks that a judge order the state to set aside mail ballots from voters "identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens," and to verify their citizenship status before their ballot is counted.Non-citizens are barred from voting in federal elections. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, in a post on X on Wednesday, said, in anticipation of the suit, "More dangerous nonsense from a President losing his grip on reality.""Trump is now demanding that California election officials VIOLATE federal law," Newsom wrote. "Apparently, the rule of law only matters when it's convenient for MAGA's dear leader. California's elections are NOT Donald Trump's to control. We will ensure EVERY California voter can participate in a free and fair election.The suit in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles came two days after acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, in a letter to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, gave the state 48 hours to determine whether any U.S. citizens were on a list of people the DOJ believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots for the Nov. 3 election.The DOJ previously gave officials in Los Angeles County a thumb drive containing the questioned names to officials in Los Angeles County. McCotter told Weber the state needed to tell local election officials to segregate mail ballots until the citizenship status of their voters could be determined, and not send a ballot to anyone who had not yet received one."If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," McCotter said in his letter.Weber's office, in a statement on Thursday, said, "In July of this year, President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullen made (still) unsubstantiated claims that California had 190,000 non-citizens on its voter rolls.""Given the many high-profile examples of states purging US citizens from their voter rolls based on DHS/SAVE data, SOS immediately requested written information about their methodology and data sources to back up their claims," Weber's office said. "They refused and provided California with nothing.""Now the USDOJ, under threat of 'emergency' litigation, demands that California blindly trust this administration without any evidence or legal authority to justify its request."Weber, in a statement Thursday, said the DOJ's "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."She also said that California "has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State's voter rolls.""My office and California election officials remain committed – as always – to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election," Weber said.Weber's office declined to comment on the lawsuit Thursday, but pointed to a letter she had sent McCotter in response to his letter.Weber, in her letter, said, "California's election administration will continue to be governed by applicable federal and state law, not by unsubstantiated claims and outrageous demands."She said that "despite failing to send the list of alleged non-citizens to my office, you demand that we request transmittal of the list, review and confirm the citizenship status of each of the approximately 20,000 individuals on the list on the eve of an election and within a mere 48 hours.""This is an emergency of the DOJ's creation," Weber said.

schema.headline: U.S. sues California in fight over checking citizenship of mail voters

title: Wholesale prices jumped 6.3% annually in September, biggest gain since 2022
description: September's producer price index came in much hotter than economists forecast on Thursday, underscoring the continued inflationary pressure from energ
body: September's producer price index came in much hotter than economists forecast on Thursday, underscoring the continued inflationary pressure from energy amid the U.S. war with Iran.The measure of underlying inflation pressures climbed 1.3% in September and 6.3% on an annual basis, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That marked the largest monthly and annual gains since March 2022 and December 2022, respectively.Both readings topped expectations of economists polled by Dow Jones, who forecast an advance of 0.6% on the month and 5.5% annually.Energy drove a sizable chunk of those increases as the Middle East conflict curtailed oil supply and sent prices surging. The so-called core PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices from the wholesaler inflation index, added 0.7% on the month and 5% over the 12-month period.But there are signs that soaring energy prices are having downstream effects on other categories. The BLS said in Thursday's release that almost half of September's increase in processed goods for immediate demand was connected to the rise in diesel fuel prices.It's the latest report in recent days showing that inflation continues to hit consumers and companies.Wednesday's consumer price index release showed a rise of 0.6% from August to September and 3.7% on a 12-month basis. Economists polled by Dow Jones had forecast growth of 0.6% and 3.6%, respectively.Excluding food and energy, the core CPI added 0.3% on the month and 2.6% compared with a year ago. Economists anticipated increases of 0.2% and 2.5%, respectively.Wednesday's Beige Book, a chronicle of economic activity published by the Federal Reserve, had the highest number of mentions of terms related to inflation on record, according to an analysis from Bespoke Investment Group.Retail sales grew 0.8% in September, surpassing the rate of 0.4% anticipated by economists, according to government data released in a separate report Thursday. That marked a slowdown from a month prior, when retail sales rose by more than 1%.Excluding spending on autos and gas stations, retail sales increased 0.25% from August to September, a drop from around 1.1% in the prior period. This slowdown offers a sign that high prices related to fuel are causing consumers to tighten the belt elsewhere.This week's data has left a growing minority of fed funds futures traders expecting the central bank to raise rates at its meeting later this month. Traders are now pricing in a nearly 34% likelihood that the Fed hikes borrowing costs on Oct. 28, up from under 18% a week prior, according to CME's FedWatch tool. About 90% expect at least one hike by the end of the year."With a second day in a row of higher-than-expected inflation numbers, it seems the Fed will have no choice but to raise rates again this year," said Chris Zaccarelli, investing chief at Northlight Asset Management.These reports offer some of the final insights into the pace of inflation in the U.S. ahead of the midterm election, which could impact how much power each political party has in Washington.

schema.headline: Wholesale prices jumped 6.3% annually in September, biggest gain since 2022

title: Tesla reveals next-generation Roadster after almost a decade of delays
description: Tesla CEO Elon Musk during a state dinner in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Sept. 24, 2026.Annabelle Gordon | Bloomberg | Getty Image
body: Tesla CEO Elon Musk during a state dinner in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Sept. 24, 2026.Annabelle Gordon | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesTesla showed off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car. The event was livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco, starting at 7:55 p.m. local time, or 8:55 p.m. ET. In attendance along with Musk were design leader Franz von Holzhausen and Lars Moravy, vice president of vehicle engineering."You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," Musk said. "You're going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company."Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, was based on a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012.  The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology, such as cold gas thrusters, to enable it to hover. Musk fanatics have been gearing up for the demonstration, expressing their excitement on social media, but the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company.At the event, Musk and his team showcased a white sports car that raced up a curved ramp, then hung upside down and vaulted off it, flipping in mid-air and hovering slowly before landing on the ground.The two-seater can go from zero to 60 miles per hour in under a second, according to Tesla's timer, a feat Moravy demonstrated for the live audience.Musk said the next-generation Roadster would enter production in 2028. The price wasn't announced. Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. Executives are expected to disclose specific pricing, details and production targets.Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017, and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly."Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either. Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his own reservation and refund requests. "I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait." Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court earlier this year over a separate matter related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure. Others have kept their reservations. Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC ahead of the event that he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000. O'Connor wrote in a message that he would be attending the show and was "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making." According to filings with the Federal Aviation Administration, Tesla established a no-fly zone around the SpaceX facility where it plans to show off the vehicle. The company had to scrap a demo on Oct. 1 due to weather issues. Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.WATCH: Tesla Roadster unveil set for Thursday evening

schema.headline: Tesla reveals next-generation Roadster after almost a decade of delays

title: Gasping for clean air: Singapore battles relentless haze as Prime Minister Wong warns of action
description: Pedestrians walk along Marina Bay as thick haze obscures the Merlion park and surrounding skyline in Singapore on October 14, 2026. The city-state exp
body: Pedestrians walk along Marina Bay as thick haze obscures the Merlion park and surrounding skyline in Singapore on October 14, 2026. The city-state experiences reduced visibility amid concerns over transboundary haze from forest and land fires in neighbouring Indonesia. (Photo by Vachira Vachira/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesSingapore continues to grapple with severe haze as smoke from wildfires in neighboring Indonesia drifts into the city-state, with Prime Minister Lawrence Wong warning of action against companies responsible for the fires. Air quality in Singapore remained unhealthy on Thursday, as smoke from widespread fires in Indonesia's Kalimantan region continued to drift toward the city-state, according to the National Environment Agency.Singapore's air quality first deteriorated to unhealthy levels on Sept. 4, the first time in nearly three years, according to government data. The worsening haze has cast a shadow over the city-state, disrupting daily life and threatening businesses as air pollution continues to worsen.In a post on X Thursday night, Wong said the government was looking into companies potentially responsible for the forest and peatland fires in Indonesia. He said authorities could take legal action under Singapore's Transboundary Haze Pollution Act where warranted, while also exploring joint action with other countries.watch nowSingapore's Seletar Airport has seen 16 diversions due to low visibility, spokespeople for Changi Airport Group and the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore told CNBC in a joint media reply.The prolonged haze is taking a toll on daily life and businesses, with some outdoor dining establishments, including outdoor dining restaurants and hawker centers, reporting a drop in business, according to the local media.  A spokesperson from Marina Bay Sands told CNBC via email that "certain outdoor experiences that involve prolonged exposure to the outdoors have been temporarily suspended" and the hotel is providing masks and air purifiers to guests.Singapore's Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Thursday that the haze was "not the best way to welcome our international guests," as the city-state hosts Singapore International Cyber Week. The event has drawn a record turnout of more than 15,000 visitors from over 100 countries. Teo said the government had begun preparations weeks earlier to support residents, including distributing masks to those most in need. While it remains unclear when the haze will improve, she said Singapore has been in close contact with Indonesian officials to understand their needs and stands ready to provide assistance.A spokesperson of ride-hailing and delivery platform Grab told CNBC via email that they have been distributing masks and have issued advisories to their platform workers as well. The haze has extended beyond Singapore, affecting neighboring Malaysia as well.Malaysia's Second Finance Minister Amir Hamzah Azizan told CNBC on Wednesday that the worsening haze requires a coordinated response across Southeast Asia, saying the country has offered to deploy water bombers and other resources to help tackle the issue. "It is an issue that needs an ASEAN solution," he said.

schema.headline: Gasping for clean air: Singapore battles relentless haze as Prime Minister Wong warns of action
